title: The language of the press
seoTitle: Turkish newspaper headlines and news style
intro: A Turkish newspaper is written in a register of its own. Headlines leave out whatever the reader can rebuild; reports name a source for every claim and choose their reporting verb with care; the passive keeps the event in front and the people behind it out of sight; and figures, dates and abbreviations come with suffixes that follow the way they are read aloud. This unit takes the four apart, so that a front page reads as easily as a conversation.

blocks.text: A headline (*başlık*; on the front page, the *manşet*) is a sentence with its scaffolding removed. The copula and `-DIr` go first; then often the subject, which the photo or the line above makes clear; and sometimes the verb itself, when a case ending says enough. What is left is a noun phrase, a short sentence or a speaker and a quote, and each shape says something of its own.

blocks.caption: The shapes of a headline
head: Shape
Example
What it says
rows: **A new price rise for petrol**: the dative marks what is affected; *yapıldı* is understood
**Statement on transport from the municipality**: the ablative names the source
a route, or a message sent from one side to another
a state; formal prose would write *soğuk olacak* or *soğuktur*
something that has happened, usually today or yesterday
something planned or about to happen: the headline's **will**
a decision announced for the future
a statement in the speaker's words, with the copula dropped
a rumour or a discovery: soft news, gossip, clickbait

blocks.text: **Tense.** `-DI` is the default for what has happened. `-(I)yor` with a time word is the usual way to announce what is about to happen: *Okullar pazartesi açılıyor* is **Schools open on Monday**, not **are opening now**. `-(y)AcAk` reports a decision or a plan, often an official one: *Köprü iki gün trafiğe kapatılacak*.

**Under the headline.** Below the headline comes the *spot*, the newsroom's word for the one- or two-line summary, and then the first paragraph (*giriş*). There the grammar comes back: full sentences, `-DI` for what has happened, and a source for every claim (next section). Hard news does not use `-mIş` for hearsay; it says where the information comes from. `-mIş` in a headline or a lead belongs to soft news, usually with *iddiaya göre* (reportedly): *İddiaya göre ünlü çift ayrılmış.* The other `-mIş` of headlines is the clickbait discovery: *Meğer yıllardır yanlış yapıyormuşuz!* ([C1 unit 7](gp-meger)).

items.en: A new price rise for petrol
items.note: In full: *Benzine yeni bir zam yapıldı.*

items.en: Schools open on Monday
The bridge has opened to traffic
Statement on transport from the municipality
Governor's office: schools closed tomorrow
Famous couple have reportedly split up

blocks.text: With a time word, the headline `-(I)yor` is a near future, as in English **Schools open on Monday**. *Okullar pazartesi açılıyor* does not mean the schools are opening as you read.
To check that you have understood a headline, say it as a full sentence: *Benzine yeni zam* → *Benzine yeni bir zam yapıldı*; *Hava yarın da soğuk* → *Hava yarın da soğuk olacak*.

sections.title: Who said it: reporting verbs and attribution

blocks.text: A news report keeps telling you where each claim comes from. A statement is reported as a noun clause in `-DIk` or `-(y)AcAk` with a possessive and the accusative ([B2 unit 4](gp-dik-clauses)), followed by a reporting verb. *Söyledi* is the everyday one; the press prefers a wider set, and the choice is not neutral.

blocks.caption: Reporting verbs of the press
head: Verb
Meaning
What it tells you
rows: an official statement, a decision, figures
a point made in a statement; the most frequent of all
the same, a little more formal
adds a point, often a fact or a figure
the point the speaker insisted on
a wish, a worry or a demand
a fact the reader may have forgotten
the last point of a statement
accepts that a report is true
the reporter does not vouch for it

blocks.text: **The sentence of a report.** The speaker comes first, with title and name, then often a comma: news style puts one after a subject whose verb is far away. The circumstances follow, very often with *yaptığı açıklamada* (in the statement he or she made), then the clause and the reporting verb: *Belediye Başkanı Selin Aydın, dün yaptığı açıklamada çalışmaların hafta sonu biteceğini belirtti.* From the second mention on, the surname is enough: *Aydın, …*

**Quotes.** A quote is followed by *dedi* or, very often in the press, *diye konuştu* (said, literally spoke saying): *“Çalışmalar sürüyor.” diye konuştu.* A long quote is announced with *şunları söyledi:* (said the following) and a colon. Punctuation follows [B1 unit 12](gp-direct-speech).

**According to whom.** *X'e göre*, *X'in açıklamasına göre* (according to X's statement), *edinilen bilgiye göre* (according to information obtained), *kaynaklara göre* (according to sources) and *iddiaya göre* (allegedly) open a sentence with its source. *Öğrenildi* (it was learned) closes one: *Toplantının ertelendiği öğrenildi.*

**What is expected.** The future of the news is mostly an expectation, and it has its own formulas: *-mAsI bekleniyor* (is expected to), *-mAsI planlanıyor* (is planned), *-mAsI öngörülüyor* (is forecast), *-(y)AcAğI belirtildi* (it was stated that … will). *Fiyatların ocakta yeniden artması bekleniyor* is **Prices are expected to rise again in January**.

items.tr: Belediye Başkanı Selin Aydın, çalışmaların hafta sonu biteceğini belirtti.
items.seg: Belediye Başkanı Selin Aydın, çalışma|lar|ın hafta sonu bit|eceğ|i|n|i belirt|ti.
items.en: Mayor Selin Aydın stated that the work would be finished at the weekend.

items.tr: Yetkililer, suyun akşam saatlerinde geleceğini açıkladı.
items.seg: Yetkili|ler, su|y|un akşam saat|ler|i|n|de gel|eceğ|i|n|i açıkla|dı.
items.en: Officials announced that the water would come back in the evening.
Prices are expected to rise again in January.

items.tr: Edinilen bilgiye göre toplantı gelecek haftaya ertelendi.
items.seg: Edin|il|en bilgi|y|e göre toplantı gelecek hafta|y|a ertele|n|di.
items.en: According to information obtained, the meeting has been postponed to next week.
The company denied the claims.

blocks.text: *Belirtti*, *açıkladı* and *kaydetti* report without judging. *İddia etti* and *öne sürdü* keep the reporter at a distance; a report that uses them for a fact everyone accepts is taking sides, and one that uses *belirtti* for a contested claim is taking the other side.
*-mAsI bekleniyor* is the news future, much like French **devrait**: *Les prix devraient augmenter* = *Fiyatların artması bekleniyor*.

sections.title: Nobody did it: the passive of the news

blocks.text: The press puts the event first and the people involved in the background, and the passive ([B1 unit 10](gp-passive)) is its main tool. Who announced, decided or reported is either obvious, unknown or not the point.

blocks.caption: Passives of the news
head: Form
Meaning
rows: was announced, was reported, was stated

blocks.text: **A clause as the subject.** With a passive reporting verb, the noun clause is the subject, so it takes no accusative ([B2 unit 4](gp-clause-as-subject)): *Toplantının ertelendiği açıklandı* (it was announced that the meeting had been postponed), not *ertelendiğini açıklandı*. Compare the active: *Belediye, toplantının ertelendiğini açıkladı*.

**The verbs of happening.** News has four ways of saying **it happened**, nearly always as a participle in `-(y)An`: *olmak* (neutral), *meydana gelmek* (an accident, an earthquake, damage), *yaşanmak* (anything that took place: *yaşanan gelişmeler*, the developments) and *gerçekleşmek* (a planned event took place). *Dün akşam meydana gelen kazada yaralanan olmadı* is a typical lead: no one was hurt in the accident that happened last night.

**Impersonal passives.** Reports of meetings use the passive of intransitive verbs: *Toplantıda ulaşım ücretleri üzerinde duruldu* (the meeting focused on transport fares), *Konuyla ilgili bir karar verilmedi* (no decision was taken on the matter). With *tarafından*, the agent appears mostly as a source: *Belediye tarafından yapılan açıklamada…* (in the statement made by the municipality).

items.tr: Yeni kütüphane dün düzenlenen bir törenle hizmete açıldı.
items.seg: Yeni kütüphane dün düzenle|n|en bir tören|le hizmet|e aç|ıl|dı.
items.en: The new library was opened to the public yesterday at a ceremony.
It was announced that the meeting had been postponed by a week.

items.tr: Belediye tarafından yapılan açıklamada, çalışmaların sürdüğü belirtildi.
items.seg: Belediye tarafından yap|ıl|an açıklama|da, çalışma|lar|ın sür|düğ|ü belirt|il|di.
items.en: In a statement by the municipality, it was stated that the work was continuing.

items.tr: Dün akşam meydana gelen kazada yaralanan olmadı.
items.seg: Dün akşam meydana gel|en kaza|da yarala|n|an ol|ma|dı.
items.en: No one was hurt in the accident that happened last night.
The meeting focused on transport fares.

blocks.text: Outside the formula *X tarafından yapılan açıklamada*, a passive with *tarafından* sounds heavy. To say who decided, news style simply uses the active: *Belediye, ücretsiz ulaşım kararı aldı*.
Read the last word of a news sentence first: *açıklandı*, *bildirildi*, *bekleniyor* or *öne sürüldü* tells you how far the paper stands behind everything before it.

Print writes most numbers in digits. A suffix then follows an apostrophe ([A1 unit 5](gp-apostrophe)) and the way the number is read: say it in your head, take the last word and harmonize with it. *2026* is *iki bin yirmi altı*, so *2026'da*; *1923* ends in *üç*, so *1923'te*.

Thousands take a dot and decimals a comma: *1.500*, *2,5*. The percent sign comes before the number, with no space ([B2 unit 5](gp-fractions-percent)). An ordinal takes either a full stop (*5. kat*, *XX. yüzyıl*, *II. Mahmut*) or an apostrophe and the suffix (*5'inci*), never both: TDK writes *8'inci*, not *8.'inci*. Times are written with a dot: *14.30'da*. A month takes a capital only inside a full date ([A1 unit 11](gp-dates)): *1 Kasım 2026'da*, but *kasımda*.

**Abbreviations.** TDK gives four rules. An abbreviation in capitals takes the suffix that suits the name of its last letter: *TDK* ends in *ke*, so *TDK'ye*, *TDK'nin*. One read as a word takes the suffix of that word: *NATO'ya*, *UNESCO'nun*. One in small letters takes the suffix of the full word: *km'lik* (*kilometrelik*), *kg'dan* (*kilogramdan*). One that ends in a full stop takes its suffix without an apostrophe: *vb.leri*.

items.en: Prices rose by 15% in 2026.
The rent went up by 15% to 20,000 lira.

items.tr: Yeni yönetmelik bugün Resmî Gazete'de yayımlandı.
items.seg: Yeni yönetmelik bugün Resmî Gazete'|de yayımla|n|dı.
items.en: The new regulation was published in the Official Gazette today.
The results will be announced on TRT at 10.30.

items.tr: Kentin nüfusu 1990'dan beri iki katına çıktı.
items.seg: Kent|in nüfus|u 1990'|dan beri iki kat|ı|n|a çık|tı.
items.en: The city's population has doubled since 1990.

blocks.text: Abbreviations never soften: TDK writes *TÜBİTAK'ın* and *RTÜK'e*, not *TÜBİTAĞ'ın*. And a name of an institution written out in full takes no apostrophe at all, while its abbreviation does: *Türk Dil Kurumuna*, but *TDK'ye*.

summary: Headlines drop the copula and often the verb: *Benzine yeni zam*, *Belediyeden açıklama*, *Hava yarın da soğuk*.
In a headline, `-DI` is what has happened, `-(I)yor` with a time word what is about to happen, `-(y)AcAk` a plan; `-mIş` belongs to rumour and clickbait.
Reporting verbs carry the paper's stance: *belirtti*, *açıkladı*, *kaydetti* report; *iddia etti*, *öne sürdü* keep their distance; *doğruladı* and *yalanladı* confirm and deny.
The news future is an expectation: *-mAsI bekleniyor*, *-mAsI planlanıyor*.
With a passive reporting verb, the clause is the subject and takes no accusative: *ertelendiği açıklandı*.
*Meydana gelen*, *yaşanan*, *düzenlenen*, *gerçekleşen*: the participles of what happened.
Numbers and abbreviations take the suffix of the way they are read: *2026'da*, *%15'lik*, *TDK'ye*, *NATO'ya*, *km'lik*.
